result.text: The sales clerks in a bank can use their software frontend to receive the credit-scoring for a certain customer.
This starts a process in the banking system which communicates with the agency in the background.
This process sends a scoring request to the agency right after the beginning.
Then, the Agency does a first quick scoring (level 1).
This will often lead to an immediate result which is then returned directly to the banking system within seconds.
The banking process presents the result to the clerk sitting at the frontend.
Sometimes the scoring cannot be determined immediately and takes longer.
In this case the agency informs the banking process of the delay and then starts the level 2 scoring (which can take up to a couple of minutes).
After the scoring result is determined, the information is sent back to the banking process.
The banking process displays a message to the clerk when he receives information about the delay to check again later.
As soon as the result arrives, it can be seen at the frontend.

result.rule: Direct each message flow from sender to receiver. Its endpoints must belong to different pools and be valid interaction nodes.
Create bpmn:collaboration when distinct participants interact and represent every participant as a bpmn:participant pool.
Do not create separate pools for ordinary internal roles unless the description treats them as independent communicating participants.
Distinguish message tasks from message events: a task models performed work; an event models a message occurrence affecting flow.
A white-box participant references its process with processRef. A black-box participant has no processRef and no modeled internal workflow.
Several unconditional outgoing flows from one activity can all proceed. Use a gateway when the description requires a decision or synchronization.

result.rule: When the description says a user-facing interface, distinct from the back-end process, is operated by a person who is not part of the process owner, starts the back-end process with a request, and afterwards gets back its outcome or notices from that process: Model the user-facing interface as its own bpmn:participant pool in the same collaboration as the back-end process. Add a message flow from the interface pool to the start event that the request triggers. For each outcome or notice the description says the back-end sends back to the interface, add a message flow from the sending task in the back-end pool to the interface pool. Keep the back-end's internal steps inside its own pool, and do not model the interface's receipt as a task or event inside the back-end pool.

When the description is written from the first-person view of a performing role that sends a request to an external party, and that party then acts on its own by paying, objecting, or letting a deadline pass, so the performing role must react to what the party does: Model the performing role as its own bpmn:participant pool and the external party as a separate bpmn:participant pool in the same collaboration. Connect the request sent by the performing role to the external party with a message flow, and connect the payment or objection returned by the external party back to the performing role with a message flow. Keep the performing role's internal steps, such as checking the case and closing it, inside its own pool.

When The description states that a party performs an action of its own (for example, a customer giving feedback after a case is closed) and names no message, timer, or condition that the process waits for.: Model that stated action as a task that represents the performed work, placed in the order the description gives. Do not model it as an intermediate catch event, because a catch event represents an occurrence the process waits for. Use a catch event only when the description says the process waits for an external occurrence.

When the description says that a process or phase begins when a participant performs an action (for example, a participant identifies a need), or that a later phase begins after a state change, and then gives the steps of the work that follows: Model the participant's performed action as a task in the flow, placed after a start event that carries no action label. Do not turn the action into a start event, an end event, or a subprocess named after its resulting state. Use a subprocess only when the description gives a multi-step phase with its own internal steps, and keep the action that initiates that phase as a separate task before it. Model the phase's final state as the end of the flow only when the description states it as the process outcome.
